question: A 6-week-old infant presents with persistent jaundice, acholic (pale clay-coloured) stools, and dark urine. Conjugated bilirubin is 8.2 mg/dL (total 10.5 mg/dL). Which ONE statement about management is MOST critical?

answers.text: Reassure the family and review at 3 months — conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia often resolves spontaneously in young infants.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia NEVER resolves spontaneously — it always indicates organic pathology (biliary atresia, neonatal hepatitis, metabolic disease, Alagille). Biliary atresia in particular is a time-critical diagnosis: Kasai portoenterostomy must be performed before 60–70 days of life for the best outcome.

answers.text: Refer urgently for surgical evaluation — biliary atresia must be excluded, and if confirmed, Kasai portoenterostomy must be performed before 60 days of age for optimal bile drainage.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in any infant >2 weeks is a NEVER-MISS diagnosis. Biliary atresia presents with acholic stools, dark urine, and conjugated jaundice from birth or first weeks of life. Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan + liver biopsy confirm the diagnosis. Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days achieves bile flow in 80%; after 90 days, success drops dramatically and liver transplantation becomes the primary option.

answers.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation and review in 4 weeks.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While ursodeoxycholic acid and fat-soluble vitamins are used in some cholestatic conditions, starting them without confirming the diagnosis and timing the Kasai operation is inappropriate in biliary atresia. This approach would allow the Kasai window to close.

answers.text: Check serum ferritin — neonatal haemochromatosis is the most likely diagnosis and requires antioxidant therapy.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Neonatal haemochromatosis is rare. The presentation described — acholic stools + dark urine + conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia at 6 weeks — is classic for biliary atresia. Acholic stools are the KEY feature that demands urgent surgical referral.

overallFeedback.feedback: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia NEVER resolves spontaneously — always investigate. Acholic stools + dark urine + conjugated jaundice at 6 weeks = biliary atresia until excluded. The Kasai window: operate before 60 days for the best outcome. After 90 days, the window effectively closes.

Correct. The Kasai window is one of the most time-critical concepts in paediatric surgery. Conjugated jaundice in ANY infant is always pathological and demands urgent investigation. Acholic stools = biliary atresia until proven otherwise. Before 60 days = Kasai; after 90 days = likely transplant.
